title: Lexical
body:
*Lexical* means "to do with the written text". Lexical scoping is the rule that **what a name
refers to is decided by where the code is written**, and can be worked out by reading the
source without running it.

```js
let x = "outer";
function show()  { console.log(x); }   // x resolves here, to the outer one
function caller(){ let x = "inner"; show(); }
caller();                              // "outer"
```

The alternative, *dynamic* scoping, would have `show` look at whoever called it and print
`"inner"`. Almost no modern language does that, and JavaScript does not, with one historical
exception: [[This]], which is dynamically bound and is the reason it causes so much trouble.
Arrow functions were given lexical `this` precisely to put it back on the same footing as
every other name.

Two consequences worth carrying:

- Because the binding a function refers to is fixed by position, the engine can tell which
  outer variables an inner function needs and must keep them alive. That is a [[Closure]].
- Because it is decided statically, a compiler or [[Module Bundler]] can analyse it. This is
  the same property that lets [[Tree Shaking]] work on ES modules and not on
  [[CommonJS]]'s runtime `require`.

The C++ version of this rule is in [[Variable Scope]], which owns the braces-and-compile-time
half of the story; [[Variable Lifetime]] owns the other half. See [[JS Functions]].
